doc.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

title: How the Miles band developed material from a small repertoire
summary: Carter describes the band's discussions and how a library of 15 to 20 tunes let them reshape forms, including modal tunes like So What.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: Was there any talking about what you were trying to do beforehand or was it evolving as you played?

Well there was conversation inasmuch as we’d say well that didn’t work, maybe if we move it over here maybe that would work. Or some of them may question, if we play double time, are we cutting the bars in half or are we still making the bars stay as they are only with eighth notes as being important rather than quarter notes being important. Do we want to change keys? Maybe we’re in the wrong key, do we want to maybe not do this? Those kind of general questions were always a part of our conversation. One thing © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

that helped us develop whatever it is, finally discussed and what was developed, was that we made a small library. We played maybe 15 to 20 tunes for those five years. And because we’d had a chance to play a song in its original form, as often, and get out as much as those ordinary forms and ordinary changes offered us, it gave us a chance to develop a different set of chords based on this kind of historical background of the song that we had played. And I think because we had a smaller library and weren’t forced to fight for the notes or fight for the changes or fight for the melodies every night or fight for the form, because the library was small enough to allow us the latitude — we knew this form. We’d been playing this form for a year. So if we make the form go like this we still know that it started out like this and had this one year intense exposure to this tune. So I think that’s part of this discussion that we would have. But it wouldn’t be through a lab and microscope, say he may take this out.

Was it kind of shock to go from, you know jazz musicians spend a lot of time learning songs with lots of changes and how to negotiate all that and the bop, and then to go and have a tune like “So What,” where you have two chords. Was it like, wow, this is really something different?

Well maybe for the musicians of 1959, but by the time ’63 had rolled around it had been thrown around enough times at jam sessions and gigs that some people understood what the choices were, and that for as many choices as there were that would eliminate some of them. So for us it was, what are the best ones of the choices, and can we make them sound musical and reasonable every night.
